title: What is a liquidity lock, and why it matters
seoTitle: What Is a Liquidity Lock and Why It Matters | CRYPY
description: Who can pull the money out of a token's trading pool? Learn how liquidity is held, what burned and locked liquidity mean, and what a lock does not protect.
summary: Who can pull the money out of a token's pool, and what a lock really protects.
inShort: A token's pool holds the coins buyers paid in. Whoever holds the pool's share tokens can withdraw them.
Burned or locked shares can't be withdrawn, or not until the lock ends.
A lock doesn't stop an owner from minting, raising taxes or selling their own tokens.

blocks.text: On exchanges like Uniswap and PancakeSwap, a token trades against a pool that holds two assets, for example the token and ETH or BNB. Whoever adds liquidity receives **pool shares** (LP tokens, or a position NFT on newer pool designs) that can later be exchanged back for their part of the pool.
When people buy the token, they put ETH or BNB into the pool. Whoever holds most of the pool shares can take most of that out.

In a rug pull, the people behind a token withdraw the pool's liquidity in one transaction. The price collapses and holders can't sell for anything meaningful. It is one of the most common ways token buyers lose money.

items: **Burned:** the pool shares were sent to an address nobody controls. That liquidity can never be withdrawn.
**Locked:** the shares sit in a lock contract until a set date. Check the end date: a lock ending next week protects little.
**Held by a multisig or timelock:** several signers, or a delay, stand between the shares and a withdrawal. Better than one person, but not the same as locked.
**Held by a wallet or the owner:** can be withdrawn at any moment.

blocks.text: A contract that only calls itself a lock isn't proof. CRYPY counts a lock only when it is a lock contract on its checked list, and reads the end date from that contract.

sections.heading: What a lock does not protect

blocks.text: A liquidity lock only stops the locked shares from being withdrawn. It doesn't stop the owner from minting new tokens and selling them, raising the sell tax, blocking sales or dumping a large supply they hold. Check those risks too: see [How to check if a token is a scam](guide:check-token-scam).

sections.heading: Check who holds a token's liquidity

blocks.text: The [Token Security Scanner](tool:token-security) lists a token's pools and, for each pool, who holds the shares it could find: burn addresses, lock contracts with their end dates, multisigs, farms, the owner and plain wallets. Shares it can't attribute are shown as not found, never counted as safe.

faq.q: Is burned liquidity better than locked?
faq.a: Burned liquidity can never be withdrawn, so it is permanent. A lock protects only until its end date.

faq.q: Does a liquidity lock mean a token is safe?
faq.a: No. It covers one risk. Owners can still mint, change taxes or sell their own tokens.

faq.q: Why does the check say some holders were not found?
faq.a: Finding every holder of a pool needs its full history, which free data sources don't always provide. CRYPY shows that part as not checked rather than guessing.
